summary.text: Take \(n=7\). Since the prescribed choices force \(x\ge 3\), the ordering \(x\le y\le z\) implies \(x+y+z\ge 3x\ge 9\), contradicting \(x+y+z=7\); thus the strengthened representation claim already fails before any primality conditions are considered.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S=\{3,4,6,10,15\}.
\]
The conjecture is a conjunction of two universal claims. Its second, stronger-looking clause says that for every integer \(n>6\), there exist positive integers \(x,y,z\) such that
\[
x+y+z=n,\qquad x\le y\le z,\qquad x\in S,
\]
and such that the six numbers
\[
2x-1,\quad 2y-1,\quad 2z-1,\quad 2xy-1,\quad 2xz-1,\quad 2yz-1
\]
are prime. We disprove this clause, and hence the whole conjecture, by taking \(n=7\).

Certainly \(7>6\). Suppose, for contradiction, that the asserted representation existed for \(n=7\). Thus there would be positive integers \(x,y,z\) satisfying
\[
x+y+z=7,
\]
with
\[
x\le y\le z
\]
and
\[
x\in\{3,4,6,10,15\}.
\]
The primality assumptions may also be included, but they will not be needed: the elementary size conditions alone are impossible.

Since every member of \(S\) is at least \(3\), membership \(x\in S\) implies
\[
x\ge 3.
\]
Because \(x\le y\), we also have \(y\ge x\ge 3\). Moreover, from \(x\le y\le z\) we obtain \(z\ge y\ge x\ge 3\). Therefore
\[
x+y+z\ge 3+3+3=9.
\]
Equivalently, since both \(y\) and \(z\) are at least \(x\),
\[
x+y+z\ge x+x+x=3x\ge 9.
\]
But the required sum is \(x+y+z=7\), which would give \(9\le 7\), an impossibility.

The same contradiction can be displayed as the finite case split forced by the allowed set. If \(x=3\), then \(y,z\ge3\), so the sum is at least \(9\). If \(x=4\), the sum is at least \(12\); if \(x=6\), it is at least \(18\); if \(x=10\), it is at least \(30\); and if \(x=15\), it is at least \(45\). None of these can equal \(7\). Thus no possible value of \(x\) in the prescribed set can occur.

Consequently, \(n=7\) has no representation satisfying the “moreover” clause, before one even asks whether the associated six numbers are prime. Since \(7>6\), this is a direct counterexample to the assertion that every integer greater than \(6\) has such a representation. The full conjecture asserts this clause together with the positivity claim \(a(n)>0\) for every \(n>5\); a conjunction is false as soon as one of its clauses is false. Hence the stated conjecture is disproved.
